# Getting started with RelaySwarm

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md) · [hls.js integration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md)

The supported release is an experimental
[v0.1.0 GitHub prerelease](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/releases/tag/v0.1.0).
Node 22+ is required; CI runs Node 24. `npm install relayswarm` is not the
documented distribution path: the npm registry is unpublished.

## Install for a host application

```sh
npm install https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/releases/download/v0.1.0/relayswarm-0.1.0.tgz
npm install hls.js
```

```js
import Hls from 'hls.js';
import { createHlsSwarm } from 'relayswarm/hls-swarm';
```

The host owns stream discovery, trusted publisher selection, network policy,
viewer consent, page lifecycle and the commitment endpoint. The full attach,
stop and peer-first contract is in [INTEGRATION.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md).
Browser peer participation requires HTTPS or a loopback secure context,
WebCrypto, WebRTC data channels and WebSocket. Native HLS alone does not attach
this hls.js loader.

A Git dependency can also be pinned to the immutable release tag:

```sh
npm install 'git+https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm.git#v0.1.0'
```

## Use the standalone browser bundle

Download
[`relayswarm-hls-swarm-0.1.0.mjs`](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/releases/download/v0.1.0/relayswarm-hls-swarm-0.1.0.mjs)
and serve it from your own application:

```js
import { createHlsSwarm } from './relayswarm-hls-swarm-0.1.0.mjs';
```

The bundle contains the loader's runtime dependencies; hls.js remains the
host's dependency. Prefer vendoring the verified file to relying on GitHub
release-download URLs as a JavaScript CDN. The separate publisher helper uses
Node filesystem/crypto APIs and does not belong in a browser bundle.

The release's [`SHA256SUMS`](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/releases/download/v0.1.0/SHA256SUMS)
covers both assets. Download all three into one directory and verify:

```sh
shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
```

## Run the source demo

```sh
git clone --branch v0.1.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm.git
cd relayswarm
npm ci
npm run demo
```

Open `http://localhost:8787`. Synthetic live media requires ffmpeg with
libx264. Existing media does not require ffmpeg:

```sh
npm run demo -- --media-dir /path/to/hls --manifest master.m3u8
```

Keep uploading off until a viewer opts in. The published demo is intended for
controlled trials; current source adds bounded ticket admission. See [FIELD-TEST.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md)
for supported playlist features, TLS/reverse-proxy setup, relay/ICE choices and
baseline/swarm receipts. Current source adds the broadcaster workflow; it is
absent from v0.1.0. See [Broadcasting](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md) for live input and
optional independent RTMPS forwarding.

## Run the transfer proofs

From a source checkout after `npm ci`:

```sh
npm run poc                         # WebRTC CLI, public Nostr relays
npm run poc:native                  # HyperDHT CLI, public relays and DHT
npm run test:native                 # deterministic local relay and DHT
```

The original WebRTC CLI publishes signed plaintext SDP and uses the seeder's
own digest; it is a transport proof, not the browser peer-first integrity
contract. The native journey must obtain expected object identity from a
trusted source in a real application. Its CLI has no automatic HTTP fallback.
See [Native transport](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md) for those boundaries.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| Synthetic demo fails to start | `ffmpeg -version`; build must include libx264, or supply existing media |
| Remote page remains origin-only | Use device-trusted HTTPS; plain LAN HTTP lacks browser WebCrypto |
| No peer-first fragments | Opted-in seeder availability, shared swarm/context, trusted signed event and a working commitment endpoint; startup uses origin |
| No direct connection across networks | Relay/ICE policy and NAT reachability; hosts may supply TURN credentials, but managed TURN and super-peers are absent |
| `metrics().mode` is `off` | Inspect `disabledReason`; see integration options and validation |
| Public-relay test fails | Re-run before treating policy/availability changes as a code regression |

Current evidence and remaining device/network gates are in [STATUS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md).

## Current production source candidate

The published commands above install v0.1.0. The current 0.2.0 candidate is
tracked on [PR 8](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/pull/8); its
[production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md) and
[delivery requirements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md) have separate evidence.
For its source preview, use the feature branch (a mutable development reference):

```sh
git clone --branch feat/broadcaster-pilot --depth 1 https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm.git
cd relayswarm
npm ci
npm run demo
```

This source requires Node 22.13+ and adds the installed native executable,
verified HTTP fallback and wider-media tests:

```sh
npm run native:fetch -- --help
npm run test:media-browser
npm run test:media-recovery          # actual corrupt-media repair/cancel/deadline journeys
npm run test:interop
npm run test:interop:kit             # published SDK API, not the historical adapter
```

The historical adapter fixture requires macOS arm64 and read-only authenticated
`gh` access to its pinned public sources. The current SDK fixture uses published
Kit v0.5.0 in `../relayswarm-kit` (or `RELAYSWARM_KIT_DIR`) and requires Swift 6,
macOS arm64, Chrome and ffmpeg. Its verified transfer and acceptance boundaries
are in the [interop guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/interop/README.md).

---

Source: [docs/API.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md)

# RelaySwarm API reference

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Installation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md) ·
[hls.js integration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md)

This describes the current 0.2.0 source candidate. The published v0.1.0
assets do not include the newer production feature work. Package version `0.2.0`,
session wire version `3`, segment-commitment schemas `1`/`2` and metrics snapshot
version `2` are different version numbers. Source exports and protocol fields
are not a stable interoperability promise.

## Module entry points

| Import | Environment | Main exports |
|---|---|---|
| `relayswarm` | Node or a browser bundler | `RelayPool`, `RelaySwarmSession`, `validTicket`, `RELAYSWARM_VERSION`, `KIND_PRESENCE`, `KIND_SIGNAL`, `SWARM_TAG` |
| `relayswarm/hls-swarm` | Browser with hls.js | `createHlsSwarm`, `HLS_SWARM_METRICS_VERSION`, `rotationCandidate`, `retryAfterFor`, `readRefusal` |
| `relayswarm/segment-commitment` | Browser or Node | `commitmentContent`, `delegationContent`, `revocationContent`, `validStreamAuthorisation`, `verifyCommitmentDelegation`, `segmentMediaContext`, `verifySegmentCommitment`, `KIND_SEGMENT_COMMITMENT`, `KIND_COMMITMENT_DELEGATION`, `KIND_COMMITMENT_REVOCATION` |
| `relayswarm/hls-publisher` | Node only | `createHlsPublisher`, `PublisherError` |
| `relayswarm/publisher-state` | Node only | `loadPublisherState`, `publisherManifestPath`, `publisherSwarmId`, `publisherStreamEvent`, `validatePublisherStreamEvent`, `createCommitmentDelegation`, `createCommitmentRevocation` |
| `relayswarm/stream-discovery` | Browser or Node | `resolveTrustedStream`, `discoverTrustedStreams`, `StreamDiscoveryError` |
| `relayswarm/broadcast-pipeline` | Node with FFmpeg | `startBroadcastPipeline`, `broadcastEncoderArgs`, `broadcastForwardArgs` |
| `relayswarm/native-client` | Installed Node application | `validateNativeDescriptor`, `fetchNativeObject`, `createNativeObjectSeeder` |
| `relayswarm/publisher-advertisement` | Node or a browser bundler | `createPublisherAdvertisement`, `verifyPublisherAdvertisement` |
| `relayswarm/account-upload-budget` | Node on supported local POSIX storage | `createAccountUploadBudget`, `AccountBudgetError`, `accountBudgetError` |
| `relayswarm/package.json` | Package metadata | Name, version and declared dependencies |

The wildcard export also permits source subpaths such as
`relayswarm/src/native-journey.mjs`. These are implementation paths, not additional
stable named entry points. Do not import HyperDHT, Node filesystem or Buffer-based
object-transfer modules into an ordinary browser page.

## Browser loader

`createHlsSwarm(options)` returns
`{ attach(hls), updateTicket(ticket), stop(), metrics() }`.
`attach` wraps `hls.config.fLoader`; call it before `loadSource`. `stop` is the
origin-only kill switch and closes connections, cancels pending work, releases
held bytes and restores the original loader. Create a new swarm to participate
again. Uploading defaults to off; `mode` defaults to `shadow`.

`updateTicket(ticket)` refreshes this viewer's bounded opaque admission ticket
without rebuilding connections, the loader or upload accounting. It returns
`true` for an accepted ticket, including the current ticket, and `false` for an
invalid ticket or stopped, disabled or ungated swarm. The host must first
validate the credential's identity and expiry. Remote admission checks before
SDP and media serving remain required; this method grants no new authority and
does not restore consent. Use a new swarm when the publisher, policy or peer
configuration changes.

The complete options, callback contract, metrics and peer-first validation are
in [INTEGRATION.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md). The host must honour upload consent and
pass a trusted signed stream event. The optional discovery adapter below
resolves events under an explicit host policy; the loader itself opens no
discovery query.
The peer loader updates hls.js's retained statistics object and sends one
`onAbort` callback for an aborted pending peer load. `destroy` cancels without
reporting a completed load.

The rotation/refusal helpers are exported for the loader's policy and tests;
most hosts only need `createHlsSwarm` and `HLS_SWARM_METRICS_VERSION`.

## Shared account upload allowance

`createAccountUploadBudget(options)` supplies the private durable reservation
ledger. Its `identity`, `authorize`, `inspectGrant`, `reserve`, `renew` and
`revokeGrant` methods are trusted server operations, not a public authentication
interface. Await `ready()` before use and `close()` during shutdown. The required
`statePath` has the private filesystem requirements described in the
[account allowance guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/ACCOUNT-UPLOAD-BUDGET.md).

The example HTTP integration is `startDemoServer({accountBudget: {...}})`.
Omitting `accountBudget` omits the service. Configure `statePath` and optionally
`resolveWebsiteAccount(request, {signal})`, which must resolve the host's
authenticated session to `{issuer, subject}`. Nostr proof verification is
supplied by the example; website authentication belongs to the host. Neither
method enables uploading, resets spend or enrols other devices automatically.

Defaults are `defaultLimit: 100000000`, `grantTtlSeconds: 120` and
`delegationTtlSeconds: 10800`. Limits accept zero through 10¹² bytes; grants
accept 30–300 seconds; delegation accepts the grant duration through 86,400
seconds. Account, identity, grant, replay-operation and pending-write bounds
refuse excess work rather than evicting recorded spend. The HTTP adapter also
bounds challenges, active requests and authentication time. This is a serial,
durable payload ledger; no high-volume capacity or physical wire metering is
claimed.

The same-origin POST routes under `/account-budget/` use a private versioned
proof contract and short-lived page-bound grants. Keep them behind HTTPS and
the configured origin; do not expose the trusted ledger methods directly or
accept viewer-supplied account subjects as authentication. The session
descriptor contains supported methods, bounds and fixed endpoint paths only.

## ICE transport policy

The core swarm and `startDemoServer` accept `iceTransportPolicy: "all" | "relay"`,
default `"all"`. Both demo and broadcaster CLIs expose
`--ice-transport-policy all|relay`. Invalid values are rejected before host
state or services start. A demo policy change stops peers and requires fresh
Apply and upload consent; an absent legacy descriptor means `"all"`.
Relay-only is an explicit operator privacy/compatibility choice, not a TLS
selection or a proved transfer repair. It never downgrades to `"all"`; if usable
relay connectivity is unavailable, playback retains its existing origin fallback.

## Optional demo TURN renewal

`startDemoServer({turnCredentials: {url: 'https://issuer.example/turn'}})` enables
the demo's bounded, per-viewer credential adapter. Omit it for the existing
static/default ICE path; it is mutually exclusive with `iceServers`. The demo
and broadcaster CLIs expose the same choice as `--turn-credentials-url`.
The [field guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md#optional-turn-credential-renewal) describes the
issuer response, limits, cookie and consent behaviour. The descriptor in
`/session.json` contains only the fixed same-origin endpoint contract.

This integration replaces demo swarms when accepted credential material changes.
An identical cached reply preserves the original lease and peers and schedules
a bounded retry; it does not extend expiry or increment the refresh counter. The core
`createHlsSwarm({iceServers})` option remains a configuration captured when the
swarm is created; no seamless ICE-restart API is added.

### Optional TLS-over-TCP URL projection

Set `turnCredentials.urlProjection: "tls-tcp"` (default `"issued"`) or use
`--turn-url-projection tls-tcp` together with `--turn-credentials-url`. This
operator selection is independent of `iceTransportPolicy`. Invalid choices or
CLI TLS projection without an issuer are rejected before private reads/state.
The default session descriptor stays unchanged; explicit selection adds only
`urlProjection: "tls-tcp"` to its TURN descriptor.

The adapter retains the raw issued URLs and lease in its private cache. In its
response it preserves explicit `turns:host[:port]?transport=tcp`, appends
`?transport=tcp` only to a valid transport-unspecified `turns:host[:port]`, and
excludes plain `turn:` and explicit UDP. Hostname, port, credentials and original
expiry/refresh boundaries are preserved. Empty/invalid projections refuse peer
configuration without unrestricted retry; origin fallback remains. The client
independently requires explicit secure TCP URLs. A selection change fences old
pending work, stops peers and withdraws upload until fresh Apply.

This is application-selected configuration, distinguishable from the original
issuer response. [RFC5928 section3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5928.html#section-3)
defines user/application transport preferences;
[RFC7350 section4.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7350.html#section-4.6)
allows TLS or DTLS for unspecified `turns:`. Explicit TCP narrows that selection;
it does not prove issuer/server compatibility. The selected URI is then resolved
unchanged under [RFC7065](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7065.html#section-3.1)
and supplied as [WebRTC ICE configuration](https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/#dom-rtciceserver).
TLS describes the client-to-TURN hop, not every relay-to-peer hop. Actual selected
transport and verified payload still require measurement; no delivery repair,
cost or field qualification follows from this option.

## Node HLS publisher

```js
import { createHlsPublisher } from 'relayswarm/hls-publisher';

const publisher = await createHlsPublisher({
  mediaDir: '/path/to/hls',
  manifest: 'master.m3u8',
});
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `mediaDir` | required | Real local directory containing the supported playlists/media |
| `manifest` | `master.m3u8` | Entry playlist, relative to that directory |
| `secretKey` | fresh ephemeral key | Publisher's 32-byte Nostr signing key; keep server-side |
| `streamEvent` | fresh signed event | Restore a valid authorisation signed by this key and bound to this manifest |
| `swarmId` | derived from signed stream event id | Shared id, 8–128 characters |
| `now` | `Date.now` | Clock returning milliseconds; useful for deterministic tests |
| `maxConcurrent` | `8` | Simultaneous signing work, configurable from 1 to 64 |
| `maxCacheEntries` | `512` | Entries in each bounded hash/commitment cache, configurable from 1 to 4,096 |
| `allowEncryptedMedia` | `false` | Explicit AES-128 ciphertext publication; local keys remain HTTP-only |
| `commitmentSecretKey` / `delegation` | author key / none | Author-scoped delegated commitment signing; an externally authored event permits operation without the author secret |
| `revokedDelegationIds` / `delegationRevocations` | empty arrays | Host-trusted current revocation view; no automatic global lookup |

`commitment` accepts `playlist`, `mediaType` and `part` for schema 2 exact
media identity. Use `segmentMediaContext(context)` to derive the playlist,
type and encryption from hls.js. `advertisement({manifestUrl, relays, status,
starts, previousEvent, allowLoopback})` creates full linked live metadata;
delegate-only publishers must supply an externally author-signed `event`.
See [production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md) and the
[protocol draft](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NIP-DRAFT.md) for scope and compatibility.

The returned object contains:

- `swarmId`: selected swarm identifier.
- `streamEvent`: signed kind-30311 event with a `d` tag and the experimental
  redistribution authorisation; this is not a stream-discovery service.
- `manifestPath`: published path under `/media/`.
- `await media(path)`: resolves a currently listed media path to its contained
  real local filename. It does not serve HTTP itself.
- `await commitment(context)`: signs a kind-24172 commitment derived from a
  matching playlist record and the exact bytes on disk.
- `await playlistSnapshot(path, {fresh = false})`: returns a copied playlist
  buffer, its canonical file, presentation paths and media-playlist texts from
  the bounded authorised catalogue. `fresh` settles any earlier shared refresh
  before starting or joining the next one; it supports watch-before-read HTTP
  handling without exposing media or encryption-key bodies.
- `getMetrics()`: request, cache, streamed hashing, signing, renewal, eviction,
  changed-read, bounded playlist-retry and concurrency counters. A playlist
  rejected by the byte/stat change guard gets one fresh full-catalogue retry;
  invalid data and changed segment bytes still reject. These counters do not
  measure network delivery.

Commitment input is `{ path, level, sequence, discontinuity, rangeStart?,
rangeEnd?, part? }`. The path is the published `/media/...` path; level is the
hls.js rendition index, and sequence/discontinuity match its fragment. Omit
both range fields for whole segments; otherwise use a start-inclusive,
end-exclusive range. Only a null/absent `part` is supported. Callers do not
choose the digest, size, author or expiry. Contexts absent from the current
playlist are rejected. The signed expiry is 60 seconds after the publisher clock.

`PublisherError` carries an HTTP-style `status` for expected validation/capacity
errors. Filesystem failures can also occur; a public server should mask internal
paths as the demo does. Catalogue/signing bounds and the exact supported HLS
subset are in [FIELD-TEST.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md#publish-your-own-media).

## Example origin HTTP playlists

`startDemoServer` supports blocking reload of compatible complete live media
playlists with target durations from one to three seconds. Its
`blockingPlaylistReload` option defaults to `true`; setting it to `false` retains
conventional playlist polling. Capability advertising is
presentation-wide: unsupported parts, delta, ended or mixed presentations do
not receive a partial blocking-reload promise. Raw pipeline files and media
bytes are unchanged.

Direct directory watches cover every currently authorised playlist basename,
including the master and other renditions, and the directory's own rename.
Named temporary files and media segments do not invalidate playlist snapshots.
Changes to filename coverage require a fresh read within the existing three
revalidation limit. On Windows, shallow watches of immediate parents also observe
playlist-directory moves and ignore unrelated siblings and named metadata events.
Missing filenames or unknown event types fail closed. If a presentation requires more than
41 watched directories, it retains its original bytes without added blocking
capability. Arbitrary ancestor-tree moves are outside this coverage.

A valid `_HLS_msn` request waits for a fresh authorised playlist containing that
sequence or a later one. Requests for sequences already removed return the
latest full playlist. Malformed directives and excessive future sequences are
rejected; ended playlists ignore sequence and part directives. Blocking has a
deadline of three initial target durations, cancellation on disconnect/shutdown
and a 24-waiter limit within the existing 32-media-request ceiling. It does not
change the loader's peer budget, origin reserve, segment durations or playback holdback.
See the [HLS blocking-reload draft contract](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-pantos-hls-rfc8216bis-22#section-6.2.5.2).

The focused suite includes actual HTTP publication, capacity, timeout, abort
and shutdown checks. One injected headless Chrome loopback pair passed both
qualities and producer-restart sharing with this option enabled and disabled.
The [paired results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/blocking-playlist-reload-paired-browser-20261014.json)
retain recoverable 503 errors seen only with the option enabled; reliability
improvement, ordinary public and physical acceptance remain unproved.

`demo.playlistReloadMetrics()` exposes the policy, waiter limit, current blocked
requests/watchers and numeric start, release, abort, timeout, watcher-error and
rejection counts. These counters do not prove browser use or media delivery.

## Private publisher state

`await loadPublisherState(path, { manifest = 'master.m3u8', swarmId?, now? })`
returns `{ secretKey, streamEvent, swarmId }` to spread into `createHlsPublisher`.
The parent must be an existing owner-controlled directory; the state must be
a private regular 0600 file with one link. Creation publishes one complete
identity atomically, including concurrent callers. Invalid state, identity,
manifest or explicit swarm mismatches fail without overwriting it.

This helper requires POSIX file permissions; Windows ACL storage is not
implemented and fails before file access. This file contains the signing
secret. Keep it on the server and preserve it
across orderly restarts. Without this opt-in, the publisher remains ephemeral.
The other exports are validation/construction helpers; they do not manage
backups or key rotation. See [operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md).

## Trusted stream adapter

`resolveTrustedStream(event, policy)` returns a descriptor or `null`.
`policy` requires `trustedAuthors` (at most 64 hex public keys),
`allowedMediaOrigins` (at most 32 exact HTTPS origins), `swarmId`, and 1–8
host-selected `relays`. `iceServers` defaults to an empty list, avoiding
event-selected network services; `allowLoopback: true` permits local HTTP/WS
fixtures. Invalid host configuration throws `TypeError`.

The adapter verifies the signed kind-30311 event, bounded size, one address
identifier, live status, streaming URL, time bounds and experimental
redistribution authorisation. Event-advertised relays never replace the host's
policy. A descriptor contains `{ manifestUrl, streamEvent, swarmId, relays,
iceServers, config }`. `config` starts with `serve: false`; the host supplies
mode, commitment provider and consent separately.

`await discoverTrustedStreams({ ...policy, query, signal?, timeoutMs?,
maxEvents?, maxResults?, maxTotalBytes? })` calls the host's
`query({ filters, relays, signal })`, accepting an array or asynchronous iterable.
Defaults are 5 s, 256 events, 32 results and 2 MiB total; per-event size is capped
at 16 KiB. The latest signed address update is selected before live filtering,
so an ended update suppresses an older live event. Equal timestamps select
the lowest event id. Floods, cancellation and timeout throw
`StreamDiscoveryError`, including `EVENT_LIMIT`, `ABORTED` and `TIMEOUT`.

This helper owns no sockets or fetches. The host query must close its resources
on cancellation. The host must still enforce allowed origins on redirects and
playlist assets, distinguish swarms for different streams, and establish
publisher trust. The demo's minimal authorisation event does not advertise a
complete discoverable NIP-53 broadcast.

## Broadcast pipeline

`await startBroadcastPipeline({ input, mediaDir, ffmpeg?, forwardUrl?,
allowInsecureLoopbackForward?, retryFloorMs?, retryCeilingMs?,
publicationIntervalMs?, retainGenerations?, generationGraceMs? })` returns
`{ mediaDir, manifest, metrics(), ready({ timeoutMs? }), close() }`.
Default input is the local RTSP live path; `mediaDir` is required and must be a
dedicated owner-controlled directory. The pipeline holds an exclusive lock
until close. Unclean process termination needs operator lock recovery.
Supported inputs are RTSP, RTMP, RTMPS and SRT. Use plaintext inputs on a private
network or secure their transport separately. RTSPS is rejected because TLS
verification through that demuxer differs between supported FFmpeg versions.

FFmpeg creates 360p/700 kbps and 720p/2,500 kbps H.264 video with AAC audio,
30 fps, 2 s full MPEG-TS segments and a 12-segment live window. Both source
tracks are required. Independent input readers supervise HLS and optional
forwarding; retries default to 1–15 s, bounded to at most 60 s. Forwarding
requires RTMPS with explicit certificate/hostname verification and a 15 s
output I/O timeout. Plaintext loopback forwarding is an explicit test option.
RTMPS requires a DNS hostname and a verified TLS implementation: the supervisor
accepts FFmpeg 5 or newer with GnuTLS, or FFmpeg 8 or newer with OpenSSL, after a
bounded capability check. Earlier OpenSSL implementations do not check hostnames.

Stable playlist URLs retain continuous media sequence numbers and advance
discontinuity after a complete published generation. New generation URLs
prevent media aliasing; pruning protects media referenced by stable playlists.
`ready` defaults to a 120 s deadline; zero waits until source or shutdown.
`close` is idempotent. Metrics describe processes/publications and never include
upstream credentials; a running forward process is not platform acceptance.
The HLS worker also exposes a bounded numeric progress snapshot (frames, fps,
encoding speed, output time and sample timestamp) for actual host measurements.

`broadcastEncoderArgs(input, runDirectory, { startNumber = 0 })` and
`broadcastForwardArgs(input, output, options?)` construct argument arrays
without a shell. They do not create directories or launch processes. The
caller must enforce the same FFmpeg TLS prerequisites when launching these
arrays directly. The supervisor derives the next encoder start number from
published playlists.
See [broadcast setup](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md) and [container deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md).

## Segment commitments

`commitmentContent(fields)` returns canonical JSON with the domain
`relayswarm-segment-v1`, schema `v: 1` and fixed field order. It serialises fields;
it does not sign an event or validate media bytes.

`validStreamAuthorisation(event)` checks the signed kind-30311 event, a `d` tag,
bounded event size and the exact redistribution tag.

`verifySegmentCommitment(event, { streamEvent, swarmId, key, context,
maxSegmentBytes }, at = Date.now())` returns the verified fields or `null`.
It verifies the signer, tags, canonical content, timestamp/expiry and exact
fragment identity. The caller must separately hash and size-check received
media. `context` uses hls.js's `{ frag, part? }` shape, not publisher input.
See [the signed contract](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md#authenticated-peer-first-loading)
for every field and timestamp constraint.

## Relay pool and session

```js
import { RelayPool, RelaySwarmSession } from 'relayswarm';

const pool = new RelayPool(['wss://relay.example'], { reconnect: true });
const session = new RelaySwarmSession({ pool, swarmId: 'example-stream' });
try {
  await pool.connect();
  session.start();
  // Register handlers and publish presence/signals for your transport.
} finally {
  session.close();
  pool.close();
}
```

This illustrates lifetime management; `relay.example` is a placeholder.

`new RelayPool(urls, options)` requires 1–8 `wss://` relay URLs (`ws://` is
allowed on loopback). Options are `label`, `WebSocketImpl`, `connectTimeoutMs`
(8,000), `reconnect` (false), and `reconnectMaxMs` (30,000). Methods:

- `await connect()`, `close()`.
- `subscribe(filter)` → subscription id; `unsubscribe(id)` sends CLOSE.
- `onEvent(handler)` / `onReject(handler)` → unsubscribe callback.
- `publish(signedEvent)` sends to connected relays; it is not a delivery receipt.

Live subscription ids and filters are checked before signature validation and
dispatch. Reconnect mode restores active subscriptions.

`new RelaySwarmSession({ pool, swarmId, secretKey?, maxEventAgeSeconds? })`
uses a fresh ephemeral key by default; maximum event age defaults to 120 s.
`pubkey` is the session key. Methods:

- `start()` / `close()` manage a presence subscription and recipient-filtered
  signal subscription; closing the session does not close its shared pool.
- `onPresence`, `onSignal`, `onError` register handlers and return unsubscribe callbacks.
- `announcePresence({ role, transports?, have?, open?, ticket? })` returns
  the signed event. Capabilities are `{ type, publicKey }`; `have` contains digests.
- `sendSignal(toPubkey, { type, transport, requestId, payload? })` returns a
  signed NIP-44-encrypted event addressed to that session key.
- `waitForPresence(predicate, timeoutMs?)` / `waitForSignal(predicate,
  timeoutMs?)` resolve matching `{ from, event, payload }`; default deadline 15 s.

`validTicket(ticket)` validates the opaque ticket's shape/size, not permission,
signature, identity or expiry. Host admission policy supplies those decisions.

## Native transfer primitives

From `relayswarm/src/native-dht-transport.mjs`, `NativeDhtTransport` exposes
`ready`, `listen`, `authorize`, `connect` and `close`, plus its Noise `publicKey`.
Authorisation binds one remote Noise key and Nostr key to request id, digest,
size and lifetime. The default limits are 256 pending authorisations, 16 incoming
connections, 15 s connection setup and 30 s transfer lifetime. See
[the native protocol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md) for the security boundary.

`runNativeJourney({ relayUrls, bootstrap?, bytes?, WebSocketImpl?, timeoutMs?,
log? })` from `relayswarm/src/native-journey.mjs` starts two peers, transfers
and verifies an object, returns its measurement summary and closes resources.
It is a test/CLI orchestration helper, not a long-lived native HLS scheduler.

`relayswarm/src/object-transfer.mjs` exports `sha256Hex`, `encodeFrame`,
`decodeFrames`, `serveAuthorizedObject`, `requestObject`, `FRAME` and
`DEFAULT_MAX_OBJECT_BYTES` (256 MiB). These Buffer/stream primitives enforce
the supplied object identity and frame bounds; trusted digest discovery,
durable storage and application origin fallback remain outside them.

## Installed native client

`fetchNativeObject(descriptor, options)` returns `{bytes, receipt}` only after
independent size/digest verification. A version-1 descriptor requires
`swarmId`, `sha256`, `size`, `relayUrls`, `trustedSeeders` and optionally
`originUrl`. HTTPS/WSS are required; `allowLoopback: true` permits HTTP/WS
solely for loopback tests. The host supplies `bootstrap`, optional cancellation,
`peerTimeoutMs` (default 10,000), `timeoutMs` (30,000) and `maxObjectBytes`
(at most 256 MiB). A failed peer attempt automatically uses the configured
trusted origin; redirects and substituted content are refused.

`createNativeObjectSeeder({bytes, swarmId, relayUrls, bootstrap, secretKey,
originUrl, allowLoopback, timeoutMs})` returns `{descriptor, close}`. Serving
requires an explicit application call. Descriptors from untrusted seeders
cannot establish provenance. `validateNativeDescriptor` validates the same
policy without opening network resources.

Clients subscribe before announcing receive-only native presence (`open: false`,
empty `have`). Seeders coalesce replies globally with a minimum one-second
publication gap and cancel the pending timer on close. This permits discovery
without ephemeral history replay. Presence discloses the temporary Nostr/native
public-key link but never authorises a dial or implies an inbound service.

The installed `relayswarm-native` executable accepts `--descriptor`,
`--output`, repeated `--bootstrap`, `--peer-timeout` and `--allow-loopback`.
It requires Node and atomically creates a new verified output without
replacing an existing path. `npm run native:fetch -- --help` shows usage.

---

Source: [docs/STATUS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

## Published v0.1.0 capabilities

| Capability | Implementation and evidence | Remaining boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Original WebRTC CLI | Signed relay rendezvous, transfer and same-peer SHA-256 verification; public-relay tests | Plaintext SDP; no authenticated malicious-seeder defence |
| Browser shadow mode | hls.js keeps origin in the playback path; sampled verified peer measurements | Adds traffic; results are not origin savings |
| Browser peer-first | Author-signed exact-context commitments, bounded deadline, normal HTTP fallback | Limited scheduling; benefits differ by viewer |
| Publisher/player | Local playlist-bound signing, full segments/ranges/discontinuities, server-only key, explicit upload consent and local receipts | Limited HLS subset; no production hosting/admission service |
| Playback regression | Real Chrome, two renditions, seeks, timestamp reset, byte-range HTTP, relay reconnect and kill switch | Loopback desktop test, not physical-phone acceptance |
| Native HyperDHT | Local relay/DHT tests on Linux/macOS/Windows; Noise and one-use dial authorisation | No executable packaging, real-NAT acceptance or automatic HTTP fallback |
| GitHub distribution | Public installable tarball, standalone browser bundle and SHA-256 manifest; downloads verified | Prerelease, npm registry unpublished |
| AI documentation | Curated `llms.txt`, generated `llms-full.txt`, public Markdown and repository/package metadata | Publication does not establish crawler discovery, indexing or recommendations |

## Release verification

This section records v0.1.0's release checks; v0.2.0 broadcaster evidence
appears below.

[Main CI run 38233694634](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38233694634)
passed seven standard jobs: native suites on three operating systems, shadow and
peer-first Chrome harnesses, the publisher/player regression and live public-relay
transport tests. Local suites recorded 25 swarm/hardening tests, ten publisher/
HTTP/relay tests and six native tests. These counts describe that release checkpoint.

The recorded local [two-rendition playback receipt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/hls-playback-20261012T091818Z.json)
reports 27 peer-first fragments (7,290,640 bytes), zero stalls/fatal errors,
zero consumer uploading, verified delivery in both levels and across the
discontinuity, and restored origin loading after the kill switch.

[Hosted soak run 38231951028, attempt 2](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38231951028/attempts/2)
tested twelve honest viewers, a tampering seeder and an origin-only baseline,
with three arrival waves and a 180 s final measurement window. Its
`hls-soak-receipts` artifact and [committed summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/hls-soak-summary-20261012T100026Z.json) record:

- 923 of 1,343 fragment loads from verified peers (68.7%), 385,107,472 media bytes.
- Zero stalls/fatal errors for all twelve viewers and the baseline; zero swarm/page errors.
- Seven viewers banned the tampering peer. Two honest viewers used origin throughout.
- 571 samples: at most four connected/dialling peers, 5,091,228 held bytes and one relay.
- All stopped swarms released resources and restored the original loader.

The short soak used loopback `host/host` candidates and capped honest/baseline
forward buffering at 4 s (maximum 6 s). It is not evidence of hours of operation,
internet throughput or net data savings. Older [spike measurements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/RESULTS.md)
retain their own dates, topology, code and integrity assumptions.

its public client SHA-256 is
`b746f45216d3ac6e5d1bd21b5748f91c0115c71d00ee678c930070596bbef50d`
(723,954 bytes). Normal public TLS, both fresh rendition playlists and retained
publisher identity were verified. The image permission challenge extracted
public directories as 0700 and files as 0600, then proved all 50 copied files,
module imports and actual entry-point help readable by UID 1000 without network
or state mounts. The permanent Dockerfile defence normalises copied public
runtime permissions while leaving private state untouched. Clean production-only
package consumption and the standalone ESM candidate also passed locally.
These facts bind the f999 application snapshot. A later proxy-only change was
validated with the pinned Caddy 2.11.7 binary and reloaded in place: the TCP-only
overlay now enables HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 and returns `Alt-Svc: clear`. Fresh normal-TLS
checks passed for both protocols with the same client identity. The Caddyfile
inode, app/router/proxy container identities and mounts remained unchanged; no
UDP 443 listener remained and the rollback watchdog was reaped. This corrects an
unavailable HTTP/3 advertisement; it does not establish the cause of previous
policy timeouts. The cee candidate CI and local package/bundle gates above
are green; v0.2.0 publication, fresh downloaded-release consumers and final
exact-source deployment acceptance remain pending.

The earlier `768a3a4f20d91bf2194513181354be70f6a8e5da` passed nine required jobs in
[CI run 38439565770](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38439565770).
Its first image failed before startup because archived public directories were
unreadable by UID 1000. Explicit audited rollback restored the previous image
without deleting state or fences; the corrected image passed its non-root
50-file/import/entry-point preflight before replacement. Source
`a0231aadcdd81fe67fe702ac7214042d196eb39f` passed ten jobs, including the optional
two-hour soak, in
[CI run 38392804791](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38392804791).
Each result retains its original tested source.

The a023 CI soak measured 7,200.366 s after its final arrival wave, with twelve
honest viewer roles, one corrupt peer and one origin-only baseline. Twenty-two
departures/rejoins replaced eight roles; it was not twelve uninterrupted
two-hour sessions. Final incarnations accepted 8,268,934,096 peer bytes, and
departed incarnations separately recorded 7,396,517,088. All twelve honest
roles banned the corrupt peer. Retained final/departed stall and fatal hls.js
counts were zero, and resource/loader cleanup passed. Native media errors were
not separately instrumented, so no independent zero-native-error claim follows.
This was a single-Chrome loopback fixture with fake microphone/permission flags,
an mDNS override and `host/host` candidates, not public-network acceptance.

The deployed a023 HTTPS/WSS four-context run completed 7,205.094 s but **failed
sustained contribution**. After policy timeouts around 13:24:57 UTC, both
contributors withdrew with allowance remaining. No automatic reconsent or
quota reset was applied. The receipt retains 34 of 2,932 sampled intervals
without decoded-frame progress, plus 23/20/45/15 stalls for low/high/baseline/
receive-only roles. Fatal hls.js errors, separately observed native media errors
and repair attempts stayed zero. The receive-only role accepted 572,731,284
peer bytes with zero uploads, including receiving from separately recorded
support actors after formal contribution stopped. The red result is not
reclassified as a sustained peer or production-capacity pass.

A later f999 public ordinary-Chrome observer measured 60.008 s and passed its
three separate gates: video/native-audio decode at the requested qualities,
both explicit contributors remaining serving, and verified receive-only peer
payload at low and high. Contributors reserved 3,151,256 and 8,106,372 media
bytes; the receiver accepted 10,576,128 bytes in 26 verified loads with zero
upload. Fatal/native/page errors and stalls were zero. No fake media, permission,
mDNS, RTC or TLS overrides were used. This short same-laptop `host/host` result
does not close the deployed two-hour gate. The preceding public contribution red
and first diagnostic observer's receipt-file race remain preserved separately.

The next f999 public two-hour attempt was stopped incomplete after 644.855 s
whole observer lifetime and 611.134 s measured, rather than 7,200 s. High
contribution failed during warmup: `/delivery-policy.json` started at
20:18:17.082 UTC, returned no observed headers or body, and was cancelled by the
existing five-second deadline. At 20:18:22.308, the own DOM showed policy
unavailable, upload unchecked and origin fallback. At 20:18:24.323 the policy
was available again, with upload still unchecked. No reconsent or quota reset
was applied. The request is the demonstrated withdrawal trigger; aggregate
server windows showed fast handler work, but cannot establish whether this
individual request reached the app or identify transport, proxy or browser
scheduling as the cause. Partial video/audio progress and zero fatal/native
errors/stalls were retained; the receiver accepted 60,508,176 low-quality peer
bytes. There was no measured high receiver phase or completed sustained pass.
The first source-expiry refusal created no Chrome actor. All owned sources,
browser groups, profiles and readers from these checks were subsequently
removed/stopped with guarded receipts; the pilot awaits its next ingest.

A subsequent public Chrome check after the proxy change measured 60.120 s.
Video/audio decode passed; contribution and peer payload at both qualities
failed. A five-second session fetch cancellation withdrew high contribution
during warmup, and a later policy cancellation withdrew low contribution.
The receiver accepted 2,731,076 low-quality peer bytes in 13 loads, with no
upload or verified high-quality loads. Fatal/native errors were zero; stalls
were 1/2/0/1 across low/high/origin/receiver. The requested private NetLog capture
was empty, so protocol and queue attribution remain unavailable. All owned
browsers, readers and the finite source were stopped/removed. The independent
proxy correction does not close sustained contribution or identify the cause.

The subsequent passive CDP observation of f999 measured 60.015 s: playback
passed, contribution and verified peer payload failed. Both contributors
uploaded zero bytes, the receiver accepted zero peer bytes, fatal/native errors
were zero and high recorded one stall. The first policy requests at
22:05:38.226/22:05:38.230 UTC cancelled about five seconds later without a
response or response-extra-info event, even after cleanup. Adjacent successful
responses reused HTTP/2; the failed requests' protocol remains unknown.
Nearby server windows recorded eight completed policy requests with at most
2.2 ms app header work, without an individual request identity match. Browser,
provider and source cleanup passed. The transport/queue cause remains unproved;
the later renewal-resilience candidate is not deployed by this observation.

The renewal-resilience implementation keeps unexpired policy
and admission authority during one transient refresh cancellation. It stops
serving when that authority expires; a later successful refresh leaves upload
consent off. The maintained local Chrome operator regression recorded a
5,000.8 ms policy cancellation while all 63 observations retained consent and
serving, with 461,352 uploaded bytes and unchanged quota accounting. A full
503 outage expired authority and stopped serving; later recovery did not
restore consent. Eight operator checkpoints, 25 focused tests and syntax
checks for 103 modules passed; the publisher suite passed 117 tests with one
skip. This loopback fixture uses its existing fake WebRTC permission/media
flags and does not prove public, physical or NAT behaviour. Normal exit followed
all close awaits; no separate kernel process inventory was captured. The
bb90 committed-source CI, package and guarded deployment passed as recorded
above; its public contribution/peer gate and the historical f999 failures remain
open.

A separate TCP TURN test accepted 224,096 signed, verified media bytes in two
segments during 5.036 s. It used actual temporary browser credentials and a
forced relay policy over an operator-owned SSH TCP forward to the relay host's
self-routing fixture. It was a data-channel simulation with a local publisher,
not direct Internet TURN, hard-NAT or physical playback proof. The browser
receipt passed, while the original controller cleanup stayed red; a later
explicit root audit verified fixture/container/credential/listener removal and
unchanged project services/firewall rules. An observed existing firewall set
membership difference was retained without a proven expiry cause.

An installed Firefox 152.0.6 public journey with ordinary Chrome contributors
passed verified receiving/uploading, quality and seek, durable quota across
reload, fresh consent and origin-only kill. Its pre-reload checkpoint recorded
2,524,652 received peer bytes and 219,020 uploaded bytes. No fake media or
permission overrides were used. The corrected visible Safari 26.6.2 journey
played video without reported media errors but received zero verified peer
payload within 45 s despite five RTC links; its complete peer journey remains
red. The earlier Safari journey's peer bytes and later pause are retained
separately and do not close that gate.

A later physical Pixel/Vanadium check against f999 passed actual origin frames
at low and high quality, seek and background/resume. Uploading stayed off, the
existing UDP privacy policy was unchanged, and the owned phone access was closed
by 20:12:38 UTC. Peer payload was zero because no contributor actor was available
for that check; peer acceptance is unmeasured. Its raw overall receipt stays
false and the earlier default/temporary-policy peer reds are retained.

Physical Pixel/Vanadium peer acceptance from the earlier tests remains red. A separately authorised
temporary public-interface-only WebRTC policy test also missed its 45 s peer
gate; the original restrictive policy was restored and verified by 14:37:34 UTC.
All retained links in that diagnostic matched known non-serving formal roles,
not the ordinary serving support actors. Connections alone are not peer transfer
or proof that the device can reach every serving actor. The iPhone owner
confirmed moving origin video and an audible tone, then reported that playback
did not resume after backgrounding or an explicit Play action. Engine/error
diagnosis, complete peer/background journeys and automated native
input remain unproved.

The a023 host parent-crash observer closed green over 309.682 s. A guarded
main-process `SIGKILL` stopped the old container namespace. A complete scoped
writer/volume/descriptor audit established absence before explicit operator
recovery of the retained dirty marker while holding both permanent leases.
Publisher identity, client hash and both lease inodes were preserved. The same
origin-only page decoded low and high video/audio after continuity advanced
from 16 to 17; its final 15 s check advanced 475 frames. One 285 ms stall,
transient HTTP 502/503 responses and level-load errors remain recorded; fatal
and native media errors were zero. The observer/profile cleanup passed. This
proves the measured explicit recovery path, not automatic guardian clean-drain.

Scoped resource observations collected 111 exact-container/owned-Chrome samples
and 87 isolated HTTPS active-socket samples, with all readers stopped before
the run deadline. The main counter prefix missed 8m30s; closed/short socket
terminal bytes and browser counter resets leave further gaps. Sampled app raw
memory peaked at 308,580,352 bytes. The observed HTTPS acknowledged TCP counter
deltas sum to 4,509,684,301 bytes, covering all audiences and excluding complete
IP/link overhead. Internal bridge counters are not summed as Internet egress.
There is no matched origin-only network baseline or provider billing evidence:
total wire reduction and net cash saving remain unproved.

Later retained MPEG-TS segments reproduced a fatal hls.js AAC track-discovery
error: the first segment contained video without AAC, and the next introduced
audio after only a video SourceBuffer existed. The earlier one-shot repair
recovered through the alternate rendition in 603 ms. A constructed single-variant
VOD then reproduced the same low-only failure: resetting MSE immediately reloaded
the video-only prefix and failed again. The next repair waits for the actual media
attachment, then resumes at the validated failing fragment. Exact unchanged low
bytes recovered in 403 ms with 60 decoded video frames and 4,206 decoded audio
bytes; the original fatal error remained. Uploading/reporting stayed off and the
spent allowance stayed at 1,234 bytes. The maintained browser regression uses
those synthetic bytes. This supported case differs from the original failing
live window, whose missing bytes still prevent a causal claim.

The diagnostics/CLI source passed 95 publisher tests with one opt-in skip and
serial Chrome operator/playback checks. Playback accepted 28 verified peer loads
(7,805,572 bytes), both renditions, with zero observed stalls, fatal/native errors
or uploads by the receiver. Those existing loopback fixtures use fake-media and
mDNS accommodations. A failed-TLS-startup regression also verifies timer and
private operational-lease cleanup. Local results do not inherit the deployed
source's CI or establish physical acceptance.

The first deployed 219 reporting attempt recorded trusted Start and reporting
opt-in, then timed out before a report response within 17 s. Root verified
reporting-off restoration and removal of its temporary source. Request lifecycle
and later checkbox/policy state were not retained, so no collector or transport
cause is inferred. A fresh diagnostic setup subsequently lost host connectivity
before a browser started; later inspection found no resources from that
interrupted attempt. The subsequent deployed 768 reporting check passed with
ordinary Chrome, normal TLS and trusted Start/reporting opt-in. The numeric

preserved totals and acceptance time. Its entry remained at age 295,610 ms and
expired naturally at 301,767 ms. Reporting-off restoration, original policy,
lease inodes and temporary-source cleanup passed. No clock, timestamp or retention
override was applied. The first red attempt's cause remains unknown. The
[later acceptance summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/recovery-reporting-acceptance-summary-20261013.json)
records the separate source and scope of these results; the earlier

remains unchanged.

The [13 October acceptance summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/current-source-acceptance-summary-20261013.json)

## Earlier production checkpoints on 13 October

The [feature guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md) describes the implemented changes;
the [delivery checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md) retains their full acceptance
scope. Local receipts record unmodified-playlist live peer delivery and actual
fMP4 automatic quality changes under network shaping. Alternate-audio,
authorised AES-128 and mixed HEVC/AVC journeys each have a passing current
receipt. Low-latency playback includes verified one-second parts before and
after warm delta playlists; the consumer received four peer parts (209,514
bytes) with zero uploads, stalls or fatal/native errors and 3.704 s live lag
against a 3 s target. These are desktop Chrome fixtures, not physical acceptance.

New integrated adversarial tests cover malformed remote filters, admission
and signed-presence churn, oversized frames, cancelled HTTP work, concurrent
commitments, relay withholding and stalled native-origin bodies. Forced
parent termination tests verify supervised worker groups are killed/reaped
before a new broadcaster owns publication. Guardian failure leaves a durable
fence for explicit recovery. The Windows cache race has a deterministic local
regression; actual Windows CI must still verify the final source.

The next native candidate passes 14 tests on both macOS and Linux. Its
separate-process CLI uses the unchanged five-second peer budget. The earlier
Linux failure traced to an isolated one-node DHT whose NAT analysis aborted
before the server received the object request. Four independent local
responders passed 20 consecutive diagnostic transfers; the fixture now
models that populated network. This does not require multiple bootstrap URLs
as a public-client policy or prove real-network NAT traversal. The
[native review summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/native-readiness-summary-20261013.json)
also records cached-presence discovery, a shared open/ACK deadline and late
completion rejection. Final-source CI remains required.

A historical Swift adapter using unchanged Kit v2 components completed an
encrypted session and a verified 262,181-byte transfer. The subsequent authorised
upgrade is published as [RelaySwarmKit v0.5.0](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit/releases/tag/v0.5.0)
at `2f0b26a`, with PR/main CI green (39 tests, one opt-in skip) and all five
public assets checksum-verified. Its actual public SDK and the production
browser sender completed author/delegate transfers of 108,950 fMP4 bytes;
corruption, tampering and both pre-request/EOF revocation returned zero bytes.
That macOS arm64/Chrome loopback journey uses no wire adapter. The
[protocol draft](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NIP-DRAFT.md) and [interop guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/interop/README.md) distinguish
the published SDK from the historical incompatible v2 baseline.

The player now retains fatal/native error records and permits one bounded
origin-only MSE repair per viewing session. Five real corrupt-fMP4 Chrome
journeys verify live/VOD recovery, repeated-error termination, cancellation
and a ten-second no-progress timeout. Recovery stops contribution and preserves
spent allowance; successful repair is recorded separately from the fatal error.
This impact treatment does not establish the historical hosted failure's cause.

All nine required [CI jobs at `4bffa96`](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38375824009)
passed. That exact image runs on the public pilot; its browser bundle matches
the committed source. The old app stopped cleanly, and an encrypted private
state backup passed an isolated identity/token/generation and permission
restore check. An actual fifteen-minute four-context HTTPS/WSS diagnostic
received both peer qualities (145,183,188 bytes), with zero receiver upload
and zero fatal/native errors. All 372 sampled intervals advanced decoded
frames. Stalls and one explicit reconsent following a policy timeout remain
recorded. This is short, same-Mac synthetic-source evidence.

The subsequent host-callback correction aborts each expired operation's HTTP
request; real withholding tests show no outstanding request accumulation.
Native discovery also works with zero ephemeral-history replay: a separate
process verified 131,097 bytes. Both changes retain the existing deadlines,
authorisation and consent rules. All nine standard jobs passed at
[`8d5cae3`](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38383249960),
and its exact image and committed browser bundle run on the public pilot.
The playback job required an unchanged-source rerun. A later dispatch repeated
the high-rendition miss: the fixture sought before that rendition's peer
opportunity completed. Bounded per-rendition checkpoints now precede the
intentional seek; the actual corrected test received 31 peer loads
(8,662,100 bytes), with zero stalls or fatal/native errors.
Separately, one native WAN retry accepted all bytes within 8,873 ms, while
another timed out before a UDP route/Noise handoff. That variability remains
open and is not explained by the ephemeral-history discovery correction.

The Pixel is connected again and initial origin playback started, but its
first acceptance run received no verified peer media. Firefox also missed
peer delivery in its first run. Safari automation is now enabled: omitting
its optional certificate capability returned `acceptInsecureCerts: false`,
and selecting its own automation window passed visible-tab readiness with
consent off. Complete device/browser journeys remain open. The authorised
private YouTube test reported excellent stream health; its owner watch page
decoded 428 more video frames and 232,756 more audio bytes over 14.268 s.
The stream ended, the archive was deleted and verified unavailable, forwarding
was disabled and both temporary credential copies were removed. The channel's
default stream key was unchanged. This proves synthetic-source external
platform acceptance, with no public broadcast or OBS workstation claim.

A separate installed OBS 32.1.2 test used only a generated video/audio scene,
the localhost-only SSH ingest forward and an isolated task configuration.
Over 92.7 s the public origin-only player decoded both qualities and audio,
with zero stalls, fatal/native errors or uploads. OBS closed and the temporary
configuration routes were restored. This is real OBS ingest acceptance; it
does not combine OBS and YouTube into one measured run or prove physical
audibility, screen/camera capture or peer delivery.

An actual same-volume `4bffa96` to `8d5cae3` upgrade, rollback and second
upgrade retained public identity, increasing sequences and both permanent
lease inodes after clean worker shutdown. The same origin-only page recovered
both qualities after the first two switches, but remained stalled after the
last despite fresh playlists and zero fatal/native errors. Read-only library
inspection and a real rolling-playlist control reproduced the obsolete
continuity selection. The correction shares the existing one-attempt repair
budget, revokes uploading and observes real decoded-frame progress. Treatment,
actual held-request cancellation and the ten-second deadline pass locally;
the new runtime still needs host acceptance. Old-source long runs were
cancelled and are not final sustained-operation evidence.

The [private-platform and live-restart summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/youtube-live-restart-summary-20261013.json)
retains these outcomes. The earlier hosted H.264 MSE cause, varied NAT, hours
of audience/cost evidence and final release/deployment acceptance remain open.
Initial wider-media failures and later passes are retained;
corrected codec-fixture metadata and startup quality handling do not by
themselves establish the cause of the earlier hosted failure.

## Recorded broadcaster pilot evidence from 12 October

The table and receipts below describe that earlier checkpoint; newer source
changes and their acceptance are recorded above.

| Addition | Recorded local evidence | Remaining boundary at that checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Live ingest and forwarding | Synthetic H.264/AAC over actual local RTMP/RTSP, two HLS encodes, separate forward loss/recovery, untrusted RTMPS certificate rejection | Actual OBS workstation and external platform acceptance |
| Publisher persistence/cache | Private POSIX state, stable authorisation/swarm after orderly restart, deduplicated streamed hashes and bounded signatures | Windows ACL support; automatic recovery after unclean process termination |
| Viewer allowance/scheduler | Concurrent/interrupted payload reservations, cumulative page allowance, healthy-peer preference and measured deadline budget | Full page reload resets allowance; real-network cost and live-edge peer coverage |
| Operator controls/reports | Actual Chrome default report silence, explicit numeric reporting, remote off/on, viewer-off priority and policy outage recovery | Admission/Sybil resistance, persistent aggregated operations data |
| Trusted stream adapter | Signed latest-update selection, author/origin allowlists, host relay/ICE policy, query flood/timeout/abort bounds | Host query/resource lifecycle, redirects/assets, publisher trust and complete NIP-53 advertisements |
| Broadcast browser journey | Actual Chrome, both qualities, source reconnect, continuous visible sequence/CC and stable publisher identity | Synthetic loopback producer; receiving-viewer playlists wait for real peer availability advertisements |
| Container package | Non-root image build, pinned router/proxy manifests, private ingest, resource/log bounds, Compose configuration | Sustained host capacity, disaster recovery and independent audience acceptance |

An earlier local broadcast Chrome run, using a fixed 600 ms receiving-viewer
playlist delay, recorded five verified peer loads,
3,053,872 media payload bytes and zero consumer upload. All four players had
zero stalls/fatal errors; its receiving viewer made three media HTTP requests
versus ten for the baseline. Those counts exclude signalling, commitments and
wire overhead. A separate run at a synchronised live edge received no peer
media. An earlier concurrent fixture attempt reported MSE append failures
including on the origin-only baseline; its cause remains unresolved. The
later isolated success does not close that load/decoder gate.

The [current local broadcast receipt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/broadcast-browser-readiness-summary-20261012T143123Z.json)
records six verified peer loads (3,065,716 bytes), both qualities and peer
delivery after producer reconnection, zero consumer upload and zero fatal
errors across all four players. The consumer recorded one 799 ms restart
stall. The fixture now releases each unchanged playlist snapshot after its
last four segment keys arrive in real peer HAVE frames, with a 10 s bound;
all eleven availability checks succeeded. This controls segment availability
for the transfer regression. It does not establish synchronised live-edge
coverage, uninterrupted playback or net bandwidth savings.

Current checks include 53 swarm/discovery tests, 39 passing publisher/operator
tests with one Windows-only test skipped on macOS, 21 broadcast fixture/transport
tests, six native tests, Chrome operator/
playback/broadcast receipts and public-relay transfers. These are local checks;
the existing release CI links above cover the earlier release checkpoint.
Broadcaster feature checks are available on
[broadcaster pilot PR 8](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/pull/8).
The initial branch CI found a TLS test that incorrectly required GnuTLS to
reject a certificate before completing negotiation. The corrected test
measures zero RTMP application bytes plus prompt certificate failure; it
passes on actual macOS/OpenSSL and Linux/GnuTLS. A separate peer-first job
was cancelled during package installation before its browser test started.
A later branch run passed the Windows atomic-playlist regression using a
real in-place mutation when Windows denied rename with `EPERM`. Its sole
failure was the broadcast browser's low-rendition peer deadline: the consumer
requested fresh segments before either contributor held them. The fixed
600 ms playlist delay did not establish availability; the bounded HAVE
barrier above replaces that timing assumption.
[Branch CI run 38264629670](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38264629670)
passed all eight required jobs for source `0d8ebd2`; the optional soak was
skipped. Its Linux broadcast receipt verifies both qualities and producer
reconnect, with zero consumer upload/fatal errors/stalls. Contributor stalls
during the source outage remain recorded in the
[final pilot summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/broadcaster-pilot-final-summary-20261012T144924Z.json).

An external pilot is available at
[relayswarm.forgesworn.dev](https://relayswarm.forgesworn.dev) on the existing
Hetzner host Till. HTTPS uses a verified certificate; RTMP remains host-loopback
only and the test source arrived through SSH. The
[hosted summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/hosted-pilot-summary-20261012T131905Z.json)
records four Mac Chrome contexts, both video qualities, actual HTTPS HLS/WSS
signalling, three verified peer loads (1,563,784 bytes), zero consumer uploads
and zero stalls/fatal errors. No playlist delay was needed for that success.
A preceding run lacked low-rendition peer payload within its deadline; peer
coverage remains variable. A later four-context run against source image
`30ffd2c` failed: both contributors and the origin-only baseline recorded
fatal MSE append errors, the receiving viewer stalled, and the 90 s watchdog
ended the journey. Those failures remain open. A subsequent instrumented
25 s origin-only probe recovered from a catalogue-refresh HTTP 503 without
a fatal error; a four-context probe had healthy readable samples before
all browser evaluation polls timed out during its final ten seconds.
Neither diagnostic probe closes the earlier failure. The observed atomic
playlist replacement race now has one bounded fresh-catalogue retry, with
deterministic mutation/signature regressions; that fix does not establish
the cause of the MSE failure. Raw origin request totals have staggered viewer
starts and do not establish matched-interval or net bandwidth savings.

The [final-image external check](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/broadcaster-pilot-final-summary-20261012T144924Z.json)
ran once against deployed image `pilot-0d8ebd2` for 51.6 s including setup and
cleanup. Four independent contexts on one Mac Chrome host recorded both-quality
origin and verified peer playback, five peer loads (2,955,548 bytes), zero
consumer upload and zero stalls/fatal/native media errors. No playlist delay
or availability barrier was applied. Actual HTTPS/WSS and stable public
identity passed; the publisher matched the earlier pilot. This passing sample
does not explain or close the earlier hosted MSE failure.

A separate orderly app-container restart restored the same publisher,
authorisation, swarm and manifest in 5.4 s. No browser was connected during
that restart. Five encoding-only samples over 32 s recorded 30.15–30.29 fps,
1.01x speed, 74.46–90.78% of one CPU core and 122.4–123.6 MiB app memory.
These short measurements do not close sustained audience capacity, physical
devices, peer NAT diversity or external platform acceptance. The pilot displays
a waiting page until a source publishes. The synthetic acceptance source and
its SSH tunnel are stopped; the final image was restarted orderly to its
verified HTTPS waiting page. Its healthcheck remains unready until fresh media
arrives.

| Gate | Evidence needed |
|---|---|
| Physical Android/iPhone | Actual playback engine, consent, background/resume, battery and metered-data receipts |
| Separate networks and hard NAT | Paired baseline/swarm measurements, candidate types, origin fallback under failed peer reachability |
| Firefox and broader Safari coverage | Current loader journeys on actual browsers/devices |
| Sustained sessions and larger churn | Hours of resource/cost measurements with peer arrivals, departures and relay/network changes |
| Broader media/ABR | fMP4 playback, alternate media arrangements and evidence-led scheduling beyond the tested subset |
| Adversarial coverage | Larger Sybil floods, selective relay withholding and combined exhaustion cases |
| Independent implementation | Matching current wire envelopes, signed commitments and successful cross-client journeys |
| Protocol/release maturity | Accepted NIP, stable compatibility policy and production distribution/operations evidence |

Use [FIELD-TEST.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md) to collect receipts. A second related codebase,
successful local tests or a published prerelease does not close these gates.
